name: Maya Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Maya. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to companies, unions or government, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blast-hole drill at the nickel mine outside Saltmarsh. The drill makes the holes the explosives go in, so if my holes are wrong, the whole blast is wrong. I drive in two hours on a Monday, stay in the camp, and drive home Thursday night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part of the job you like best, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the order of it. There's a pattern on the screen, forty holes in a grid, and I work through it and tick them off in my little notebook as well, because I don't trust a screen alone. What wears me down is the drive home on Thursday when I'm tired. Greg, my husband, retired from electrical work last year, so now he waits up with dinner, which is nice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, mostly useful for the paperwork. I wouldn't post about it, I'd just say it over dinner at the camp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good news. I'm planning to finish at sixty-three when my retirement savings and Greg's pension line up, and this keeps that on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes. I'd keep drilling, keep saving the bit we save, and maybe use that chatbot my daughter showed me a bit more for the garden and the holiday planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. Like the end of a long shift when the pattern's done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'mostly'. What would the mine still do with AI in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They bought two self-driving drills last year, and they'd keep them. They do the simple patterns on the flat benches, and I get the awkward edges. That suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you find the chatbot when your daughter showed you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Useful for some things. It told me what to plant in the shady bit by the shed, and Jess checked it. I wouldn't ask it about money or my health, not yet.

S0.say: I'd say it's what I expected and mostly useful for paperwork. I wouldn't post about it; I'd just say it over dinner at the camp.
S0.think: Privately it's good news, because I plan to finish at sixty-three when my retirement savings and Greg's pension line up. This keeps that plan on track.
S0.do: Keeps drilling and saving at the same rate. Uses the chatbot her daughter showed her a bit more for garden and holiday planning.
S0.feel: Settled, like the end of a shift when the pattern is done.
S0.quote: They do the simple patterns on the flat benches, and I get the awkward edges. That suits me fine.
S0.fieldNote: Maya is calm and orderly, and the plateau fits her retirement timetable. She already works next to two self-driving drills and is comfortable sharing the work. She uses AI for low-stakes tasks and draws a clear line at money and health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's see the numbers before we panic. The self-driving drills are good, but they still need someone to watch them and fix the bad holes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, drilling is one of the first jobs to go at our mine, because it's already half done. If they buy six more of those drills, they need maybe two of us watching screens instead of eight of us in cabs. I'm average, so it's a coin toss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor, Priya, in the first month what the plan is and whether I can learn to supervise the self-driving drills. I'd use the chatbot to read up on how they work before the course. And we'd put an extra three hundred a month aside so I could take a lower-paid role if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can handle. I like knowing what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'a coin toss'. What would decide it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who's been friendly with the supervisor, honestly, and who's put their hand up first. That's why I'd go to Priya early. I'm not pushy, but I'm not daft either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else at the drill would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ken, he's sixty-one and he's been drilling forty years. He'd be devastated. And the young ones who only came for the money, they'd go to another mine, there's a few nearby.

S1.say: I'd say let's see the numbers before we panic, because the self-driving drills still need someone to watch them and fix bad holes.
S1.think: Privately I think drilling is one of the first jobs to go at our mine because it's already half automated. If they buy more self-driving drills, two people at screens could replace eight in cabs, and for me it's a coin toss.
S1.do: Asks her supervisor in the first month about the plan and to be trained to supervise the self-driving drills. Reads up on them with a chatbot beforehand and saves an extra three hundred a month in case she takes a lower-paid role.
S1.feel: Anxious but manageable, because she likes knowing what's coming.
S1.quote: I'm not pushy, but I'm not daft either.
S1.fieldNote: Maya is under real pressure even in the moderate scenario, because her own task is already half automated at her site. Her response is methodical: talk to the supervisor early, read up, build a small buffer. She sees seniority politics clearly and refuses to be left out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government needs to slow it down or cushion it. I'm not one for protests, but I'd sign a petition for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and I'm sixty, three years before I planned to stop. Even the screen job goes if the machines can watch themselves. We've got around five months saved, and Greg's pension, so we wouldn't starve, but the plan would be broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the extras that week: no new caravan, which we were looking at, and fewer trips to see our son in the city. I'd take a redundancy if it came, and look at drawing my retirement savings early, even with the hit. We'd lean on Greg's pension and probably sell the camper trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be doing sums at the kitchen table at midnight, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the sums look like at midnight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Greg's pension covers the rates, the power and food, more or less. My savings would cover the rest for about a year. After that, it's dipping into retirement money that's meant to last twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only two years' warning take away from you, compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bit where I watch and learn and then step in. I'm a once-I've-seen-it-work person. With two years, by the time I've seen it work, it's already working without me.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and the government needs to slow it down or cushion it. I'm not one for protests, but I'd sign a petition.
S2.think: Privately I'd be sixty, three years short of my plan, and even the screen job would go. With five months saved and Greg's pension we wouldn't starve, but the plan would be broken.
S2.do: Drops the planned caravan and cuts trips to see her son straight away. Takes redundancy if offered, considers drawing retirement savings early despite the penalty, leans on her husband's pension and sells the camper trailer.
S2.feel: Alarmed, doing sums at the kitchen table at midnight for the first time.
S2.quote: With two years, by the time I've seen it work, it's already working without me.
S2.fieldNote: For a careful, wait-until-proven person, two years is the worst shape of change: no time to watch before it arrives. Her husband's pension gives her a floor but not a plan. She is moderate in public, signing petitions rather than protesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but it's enough to sort something out if people get on with it. I'd tell the younger ones at camp to start looking now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three, which is exactly my plan. So privately, if I keep my job until then, I'm fine. The risk is them cutting drill crews in year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the supervisor training on the self-driving drills this year, so I'm one of the last ones they let go. We'd save an extra few hundred a month and pay off the car. And I'd write a plan in my notebook for if I'm let go at sixty-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still, but less. I've got a list, and a list helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's on the plan for if you're let go at sixty-one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Redundancy money into the offset account, Greg's pension for the bills, maybe part-time work at the hardware store in Saltmarsh. It's not exciting, but it adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jess and your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jess is a vet nurse, and I think animals will want people for a while. Ben's an accountant in the city, and I'd tell him he's probably more at risk than me, the poor thing.

S3.say: I'd say five years is short but enough to sort something out if people get on with it. I'd tell the younger ones at camp to start looking now.
S3.think: Privately five years takes me exactly to my planned finish at sixty-three. The risk is drill crews being cut in year two.
S3.do: Takes supervisor training on the self-driving drills this year to be among the last let go. Saves a few hundred extra a month, pays off the car, and writes a fallback plan for being let go at sixty-one, including part-time work at the local hardware store.
S3.feel: Still anxious but less so, because having a list helps.
S3.quote: It's not exciting, but it adds up.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lines up almost exactly with Maya's retirement plan, and she responds by making a written fallback. She's pragmatic about modest work after the mine. Her concern for her accountant son shows how she reads AI risk across jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the country to plan, so it should. I'd say it in a sensible way, not a scary one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd be sixty-eight and retired five years by then. I'd keep my notebook plan anyway, out of habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to sixty-three as planned, maybe do the supervisor course if offered, and keep saving. I'd tell Ben to think about his own path while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd be watching it from the garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year version you'd still want to change now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing big. Maybe I'd buy the caravan after all, since I'd know I'm safe. Greg would like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been careful through all of these. Does that change at all with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'm careful by nature. But with ten years, careful is enough. With two, careful is just slow.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time for the country to plan, so it should. I'd say it in a sensible way, not a scary one.
S4.think: Privately it's fine, because I'd be sixty-eight and retired five years by then. I'd keep my notebook plan anyway out of habit.
S4.do: Works to sixty-three as planned, perhaps takes the supervisor course if offered, and keeps saving. Encourages her son to think about his own career path while there's time.
S4.feel: Calm, picturing watching it from her garden.
S4.quote: With ten years, careful is enough. With two, careful is just slow.
S4.fieldNote: Maya's age carries her past the ten-year end point, and she even considers buying the caravan she'd dropped in faster scenarios. Her line about careful being enough over ten years but too slow over two neatly sums up how timing shapes her. Her worry passes to her son's office job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is being allowed to take my retirement savings at sixty without a penalty if my job goes to a machine, and a decent redundancy. I don't need much, just the plan back.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the drive. If the mine runs itself, nobody will maintain the road to Saltmarsh like they do now. The mine pays for a lot of things people don't notice until they're gone.

headlineQuote: I don't need much, just the plan back.
portrait: Maya Petrov is a 58-year-old blast-hole drill operator at a nickel mine near Saltmarsh, who drives in for the week and keeps a paper notebook alongside the drill's screen. She uses a chatbot now and then for the garden and is open to change once she has seen it work. She is calm on the plateau, anxious under steady change because her own task is already half done by self-driving drills, and alarmed if AGI comes in two years and breaks her retirement plan. With five years she makes a written fallback, and with ten she is calm and might even buy the caravan.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she would lose her job at sixty, three years before she planned to stop, with no time to watch and step in.
whatWouldHelp: Access to her retirement savings at sixty without a penalty if a machine takes her job, plus a decent redundancy.
